children: Defence Minister Rajnath Singh Calls for Strengthening Indigenous Design, Development, Testing and Manufacturing of Advanced Aero-Engines

Defence Minister Rajnath Singh witnessed the delivery of the 2,000th aero-engine by Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL), Koraput Division and announced the establishment of a second production line for Shakti engines on Tuesday. Describing the milestone as a significant achievement in India’s aerospace journey. Rajnath called for strengthening indigenous capabilities in the design, development, testing, manufacturing and maintenance of advanced aero-engines, stressing that mastery of propulsion technology is essential for self-reliance in the aerospace and defence sector.

“The delivery of 2,000 engines represents 2,000 significant contributions to the operational capability of the Defence Forces and reflects six decades of engineering expertise and technological experience since the Division was established in 1964” said Rajnath, while congratulating the engineers, technicians, scientists and skilled workforce of HAL Koraput.

Rajnath Singh highlighted HAL Koraput’s contribution to military aviation, noting that its engines have powered frontline aircraft including the MiG-21, MiG-27, MiG-29 and Su-30MKI. Rajnath stated that while production provides new capability, overhaul extends service life, making both critical for military preparedness. Rajnath appreciated HAL Koraput’s indigenous repair and overhaul capability, with more than 9,000 engines overhauled so far, and noted that indigenisation of components and reduced turnaround time are contributing to operational readiness and extended service life of critical defence assets.

“The aero-engine is the ‘heart’ of an aircraft, and reliable propulsion is essential to effectively utilize advanced airframe, radars, weapons and avionics” said Rajnath. The Minister highlighted the need for expertise in precision manufacturing, advanced materials, metallurgy, cooling technologies, testing and stringent quality assurance. Rajnath noted that aero-engine technology combines advanced superalloys, thermal-barrier coatings and sophisticated cooling systems for reliable performance under extreme conditions, making mastery of propulsion technology a mastery of some of the most advanced industrial capabilities.

Rajnath underlined that aerospace self-reliance must extend to indigenous aero-engine capability, particularly for the Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA) programme. The Minister highlighted the proposed investment of around Rs 5,000 crore, indigenisation of raw materials in partnership with Mishra Dhatu Nigam Limited (MIDHANI) and establishment of India’s first indigenous high-thrust engine testing facility. Rajnath stressed that a sovereign aerospace ecosystem requires indigenous capabilities across materials, design, manufacturing, testing and Maintenance, Repair and Overhaul (MRO).

Rajnath highlighted HAL’S performance in meeting Defence Forces’ requirements, noted that the Government placed an order for 240 AL-31FP engines with HAL in 2024 for the Su-30MKI. Despite global supply-chain disruptions and raw-material challenges, HAL delivered the first engine ahead of schedule and has delivered 63 engines against a target of 60 by the end of the second year.

Rajnath announced that HAL is enhancing annual AL-31FP production capacity from 30 to 50 engines with an investment of Rs 335 crore and also a second Shakti engine production line with an investment of Rs 218 crore. The new line will manufacture up to 100 engines annually and is scheduled to be fully established by 2028-29, catering to indigenous helicopters including Dhruv Advanced Light Helicopter (ALH) and Prachand Light Combat Helicopter (LCH).

Rajnath noted that aero-engine development is a long-term endeavour requiring sustained investment, specialised testing, skilled manpower and a strong industrial ecosystem, with focus on repeatable, reliable and scalable production, design, critical materials and superalloys. Rajnath called for greater integration of MSMEs, start-ups, private industry, academia and research institutions into the propulsion ecosystem. The Minister called upon HAL to develop Koraput not merely as an engine production facility but as a broader aerospace propulsion ecosystem by nurturing suppliers, mentoring MSMEs, supporting start-ups and young engineers, collaborating with universities and research institutions, and developing capabilities for critical components.
